lessons.title: Introduction to Arrays

content.title: What is an Array?
content.text: An array is a data structure used to store multiple values of the same type in a sequence. Elements are stored at positions called indexes.

content.title: Indexing
content.text: In most programming languages, array indexing starts at 0. Therefore, the first element is at index 0 and the second element is at index 1.

content.title: Array Size
content.text: The size of an array represents how many elements it contains. Accessing an element by index is generally a constant-time operation.

key_points: Arrays store multiple values in a sequence.
Direct element access is generally O(1).

lessons.title: Traversing Arrays

content.title: Array Traversal
content.text: Traversal means visiting each element of an array, usually using a loop.

content.title: Python Traversal
Index-Based Traversal
Time Complexity
content.text: Visiting every element once takes O(n) time because the number of operations grows with the number of elements.

key_points: Loops are commonly used for traversal.
Traversing all elements takes O(n) time.

lessons.title: Searching Arrays

content.title: Linear Search
content.text: Linear search checks elements one by one until the target is found or the array ends.

content.title: Linear Search
Linear Search Complexity
content.text: Linear search has O(n) worst-case time complexity because it may need to inspect every element.

content.title: Binary Search
content.text: Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted array into halves and eliminates the half that cannot contain the target.

content.title: Binary Search Concept
content.code:
Sorted array:
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

Target = 40
Check middle -> 30
Target is larger -> search right half
Check 40 -> found

content.title: Binary Search Complexity
content.text: Binary search runs in O(log n) time, but it requires the data to be sorted.

key_points: Linear search works on unsorted data.

content.title: Insertion
content.text: Insertion adds an element to an array. Inserting in the middle may require existing elements to be shifted.

content.title: Deletion
content.text: Deletion removes an element. Removing an element from the middle may require later elements to shift.

content.title: Complexity
content.text: Insertion or deletion at the end of a dynamic array can often be efficient, while operations in the middle may require O(n) shifting.

lessons.title: Sorting Arrays

content.title: Why Sort?
content.text: Sorting arranges elements in a specific order, such as ascending or descending order. Sorted data can make searching and analysis easier.

content.title: Bubble Sort
content.text: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order.

content.title: Bubble Sort
Selection Sort
content.text: Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and places it in the correct position.

content.title: Insertion Sort
content.text: Insertion sort builds a sorted portion of the array by inserting each new element into its correct position.

key_points: Selection sort selects the next minimum element.
Insertion sort builds a sorted portion.

content.title: Find Maximum
Calculate Sum
content.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
total = 0

for number in numbers:
    total += number

print(total)

content.title: Duplicate Detection
content.text: Duplicates can be detected by comparing elements or by using a set to track values that have already been encountered.

key_points: Maximum and minimum can be found using a single traversal.
Array sums can be calculated in O(n).
Sets can help detect duplicates efficiently.

lessons.title: Array Complexity and Problem Solving

content.title: Time Complexity
content.text: Time complexity describes how the running time of an algorithm changes as the input size increases.

content.title: Common Complexities
content.text: Direct array access is commonly O(1), traversal is O(n), linear search is O(n), and binary search is O(log n) when the data is sorted.

content.title: Complexity Examples
content.code:
Access element: O(1)
Traverse array: O(n)
Linear search: O(n)
Binary search: O(log n)

content.title: Choosing an Algorithm
content.text: When solving an array problem, first understand the input, identify the required operation, consider whether the data is sorted, and choose an approach that provides acceptable time and space complexity.

key_points: Traversal and linear search are O(n).
Binary search is O(log n) on sorted data.
